standard_prerequisites.name: Turing machine and its index
standard_prerequisites.statement: Turing machines are enumerated by natural numbers in the standard way, and M_e denotes the machine with index e; the index can be written on a tape in unary as a list of blocks encoding the instruction table.
standard_prerequisites.use: The construction starts by decoding the index e of the machine to be simulated (source lines 1448-1456).

standard_prerequisites.name: Encoding of a configuration in unary on the simulating tape
standard_prerequisites.statement: States, tape symbols and head positions are represented as blocks of strokes separated by blanks, with the symbol numbers 1, 2 and 3 for the end marker, the blank and the stroke.
standard_prerequisites.use: The simulated tape records the contents as blocks of three strokes and the head position as a counter that is extended or shortened (source lines 1456-1465, 1485-1492).

standard_prerequisites.name: The Church-Turing thesis
standard_prerequisites.statement: Every effectively computable function is computed by some Turing machine.
standard_prerequisites.use: The author invokes the thesis at source lines 1447-1448 to conclude that the described simulation really is carried out by a Turing machine, since the machine is only described in outline.

core_obligations: Describe the decoding stage: on input (e,n) the machine writes, to the right of the input, the instruction table of M_e as a list of unary blocks, followed by the number of the start state and the number 1 (source lines 1448-1456).

Describe the tape encoding: copy the input so that each stroke of the simulated tape becomes a block of three strokes, using an alphabet with fixed symbol numbers for end marker, blank and stroke, and record the simulated head position as a counter (source lines 1456-1465).

Describe the simulation cycle: locate the k-th block to read the simulated symbol, find the instruction matching the recorded state and symbol, rewrite the symbol block, replace the recorded state, adjust the head-position counter, and repeat (source lines 1461-1479).

Describe termination and output: when no instruction matches, halt the simulation and convert the simulated tape back into a single block of strokes of length m, and when the tape contains anything other than a block of three strokes, halt with an undefined value (source lines 1480-1497 of the retained span).

proof_roadmap.step: Decode the index e into the instruction table and write the start state and the number 1.
Copy the input with each stroke expanded to a block of three strokes and record the head position.
Run the simulation cycle: read the simulated symbol, find the instruction, rewrite the symbol, update the state and the head position.
Handle halting and non-halting: convert the simulated tape to a unary output when the simulated machine halts, diverge when it does not, and halt with an undefined value on malformed tape contents.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is the author's own theorem thm:universal-tm at source lines 1434-1443: there is a Turing machine U which on input (e,n) halts exactly when the machine with index e halts on n, and reproduces its output. The proof at source lines 1445-1512 is an outline construction rather than a machine written step by step, and that is how the author presents it (the source explicitly says that producing U is basically impossible and that the outline plus the Church-Turing thesis is what is offered). Its content is a simulation architecture: decode the index e to the right of the input into a list of unary blocks describing the instructions of M_e, write the start state and the number 1 next to that description, copy the input with each stroke replaced by a block of three strokes so that the simulated tape uses a three-symbol alphabet, and then repeat a cycle of steps that reads the simulated tape, finds the matching instruction, rewrites the simulated symbol, updates the recorded state, and moves the recorded head position. Each of those stages is a genuinely different block of machinery, and the last one has to handle the case in which the simulated machine halts, by converting the simulated tape back into a block of strokes. Because the argument is an outline completed by the Church-Turing thesis rather than an explicit machine, it is marked for human spot-check. No result outside the retained text is used beyond the thesis the author invokes.

The proof is an outline that ends by invoking the Church-Turing thesis, as the author says explicitly in its first sentence; the retained package therefore carries the author's own outline and not a machine-level construction, and the card records this so a human can spot-check the level of detail.
